description: Layered technical-writing standard: Diátaxis structure, Google developer style sentences, STE instruction rules, Global English syntax. Use for /technical-writing or when writing or reviewing docs, RFCs, readmes, PR descriptions, or commit messages.

compare.without: Writes steps with "simply", "easy" or the passive voice.
compare.with: Writes each step as a direct command, with the condition first.

compare.without: Writes every sentence the same length, with no view even in explanations.
compare.with: Mixes short and long sentences and takes a view in explanations.

compare.without: Pastes logs and SHA lists into the PR body.
compare.with: Writes the PR body as a one-minute briefing and links the logs.

brief.intro: It sets the goal, a tired engineer understands on the first read, then five rules: cut idle words, use everyday words, fix a sentence another way when a rule hurts it, write real names, and invent no jargon.
sections: Mixes short and long sentences, takes a view in explanations, and writes specifics like "a column rename fails the build".
One mode per doc: tutorials show a visible result each step, how-tos give only actions, reference only describes, opinion lives in explanations.
Addresses "you" in present tense, writes commands, puts conditions first, makes headings carry the point, and labels links clearly.
One instruction per sentence, a split past about 20 words, warnings before the step, and one word per action.
Keeps "only" and "not" beside their word, breaks up noun strings, gives each "it" one referent, and drops semicolons and slashes.
Runs `unslop` on every touched doc, applies the rules to PRs and commits, and leaves UI strings to product copy guidelines.

lessons.quote: Write so a tired engineer understands on the first read.
lessons.quoteTr: Write so a tired engineer understands on the first read.
lessons.title: Write for one concrete reader
lessons.does: The doc reads clearly the first time, with no need to go back.
lessons.why: "A tired engineer" on "the first read" is a picture you can imagine, far easier to aim at than "be clear".
lessons.try: For a notice people must follow, say: "Write it so a support rep finishing a night shift can act on it after one read."

lessons.quote: Use the short, everyday word: "use", not "utilize".
lessons.quoteTr: Use the short, everyday word: "use", not "utilize".
lessons.title: Follow the rule with one swap
lessons.does: It uses short everyday words by default and swaps a long word like "utilize" for "use".
lessons.why: Pairing the rule with one concrete "this, not that" lets the AI copy the swap instead of guessing what counts as simple.
lessons.try: To get plainer prose, give one swap: "Write 'use', not 'make use of'."

lessons.quote: When a rule makes a sentence worse, fix the sentence another way or leave it alone.
lessons.quoteTr: When a rule makes a sentence worse, fix the sentence another way or leave it alone.
lessons.title: Give the rules a way out
lessons.does: It won't twist a sentence into something worse just to obey a rule.
lessons.why: Saying the rules serve readability, not the other way round, stops the AI from applying them mechanically.
lessons.try: After a list of style rules, add: "If a rule makes a sentence harder to read, skip it. Readability wins."

lessons.quote: Write the real symbol, file, flag, or command name, not a synonym or a description of it.
lessons.quoteTr: Write the real symbol, file, flag, or command name, not a synonym or a description of it.
lessons.title: Use the real names
lessons.does: The doc uses the real function, file, and command names, not friendlier aliases.
lessons.why: Pointing "which word to use" at names that already exist in the code stops the AI from inventing its own.
lessons.try: For a user guide, add: "Write every button name exactly as it appears in the app."

lessons.title: One doc, one job
lessons.does: Before writing, it picks tutorial, how-to, reference, or explanation, writes only that, and splits the rest out behind a link.
lessons.why: A flat rule plus a fix (split and link) spares the AI from weighing each paragraph on whether it belongs.
lessons.try: When you ask for a doc, say: "Only the install steps here. Put the background in a separate page and link to it."

blocks: Write so a tired engineer understands on the first read.

- Cut every word that does no work.
- Use the short, everyday word: "use", not "utilize".
- When a rule makes a sentence worse, fix the sentence another way or leave it alone.
- Write the real symbol, file, flag, or command name, not a synonym or a description of it.
- Don't invent jargon. Use the words a developer would say out loud. Say what a named pattern means the first time.

- Mix sentence lengths. Split the sentence that carries two thoughts. Keep the long sentence that carries one.
- Have a view in explanation. Keep reference dry.
- Be specific. Not "schema changes can cause issues" but "a column rename fails the build".
One document, one mode. Don't mix modes. Split and link instead.

- **Tutorial: learning by doing.** Say what the learner will build. Every step produces a visible result, and you say what they should see. Explanation gets one clause and a link.
- **How-to: steps to a goal.** Solve the reader's problem. Assume competence. Action only. Allow forks. Name the guide by the task.
- **Reference: facts for lookup.** Only describe. Be dry, complete, and sure. Mirror the structure of the thing described.
- **Explanation: understanding and why.** One bounded topic. Give context: design decisions, history, constraints, alternatives. Opinion is allowed here and nowhere else.
## Write sentences to the reader (Google developer style)

- Talk to the reader as "you", in the present tense.
- Say who does what. Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or beside the point.
- Write instructions as commands. Put the condition before the instruction and the common case first.
- No buzzwords, no figurative language, no "please", and never "simply", "easy", or "quickly" in a procedure.
- Don't pre-announce, and don't start consecutive sentences with the same phrase.
- Link with words that say where the link goes.
- Headings carry the point, in sentence case. One h1 per page, no skipped levels.
- Numbered lists for sequences, bullets for everything else. Introduce a list with a complete sentence. Keep items parallel.
- Code goes in code font. UI elements go in bold. Use serial commas. Drop "etc.".
## Make statements load one at a time (STE rules)

- One instruction per sentence. One thought per sentence everywhere else.
- Split instructions longer than about 20 words and other sentences longer than about 25.
- Put the warning or condition before the step it guards.
- Keep "the" and "a".
- Give each word one meaning, and pick one word per action.
- Write procedures as direct commands, never as narration and never in the passive.
- Avoid "-ing" words where you can.
## Leave no sentence open to two readings (Global English)

- Keep words like "only" and "not" next to the word they change.
- Break up long noun strings.
- Make every "it", "they", and "this" point at one obvious thing. Never use "this" or "which" to point at a whole clause.
- Don't drop verbs, or the small words that show structure, such as "that".
- Repeat the article in a series when it prevents a misread. Say which parts "and" or "or" joins.
- Use periods, not semicolons or em dashes. No slashes, and no "(s)". Make text in parentheses a full grammatical unit.
- Call each thing by one name, everywhere.
- Skip idioms, colloquialisms, Latin abbreviations, and metaphors.

- Apply the **unslop** skill to every doc this skill touches. That skill owns the slop-pattern catalog: AI vocabulary, filler, hedging, formatting tells.
- PR descriptions and commit messages are writing too. Every layer except Diátaxis applies to them. A PR body is a briefing that a reviewer can read in under a minute. Do not paste swarm logs, SHA lists, or metric tables. Link them.
- Product UI strings are not documentation. Use your product's copy guidelines for those.
- Indent code snippets with tabs. Write real paths. Make every count or tree claim true at the commit that lands it, and include the command that regenerates it.
